blocks.title: Patents, SPCs and the launch date

summary.title: Patent types
points: A patent lets its owner stop others using an invention for up to 20 years from filing.
Layers: compound (basic patent), salt or crystal form, formulation, process, use or dosing.
Secondary patents can sometimes be avoided with a different salt, formulation or process.
The compound patent can't be designed around: the generic has the same molecule.
Compound patent plus SPC usually sets the earliest date; secondary patents decide if your product is free.

exercises.scenario: A formulation patent covers the originator's tablet, which uses a particular coating system.

questions.prompt: What might let your generic avoid it?
options: A different formulation, if regulatory work supports it
Waiting for the compound patent to expire, which also ends the formulation patent
Using the same formulation with a different invented name
Filing under a different legal basis such as Art. 10a
questions.explanation: Secondary patents can sometimes be designed around.

questions.prompt: Which patent can no generic design around?
options: The crystal-form patent on one polymorph
The process patent on how the API is made
The dosing patent on a new regimen
The compound patent
questions.explanation: The generic contains the same molecule.

exercises.scenario: The dossier team plans a change of salt late in development.

questions.prompt: Why should IP and the dossier be read together?
options: Salts aren't covered by any patent
A salt change resets the data protection clock
The salt choice may decide whether a secondary patent is infringed
The patent office approves the dossier's choice of salt before filing
questions.explanation: Design-arounds usually need regulatory work.

questions.prompt: How long can a patent last from its filing date?
options: Indefinitely, if renewed
Up to 20 years
Up to 10 years, like market protection
Up to 15 years from the first authorisation
questions.explanation: SPCs can then extend the basic patent.

summary.title: SPCs and the paediatric extension
points: An SPC extends the basic patent to make up for development time.
Length: patent filing to first EU authorisation, minus 5 years, capped at 5.
Overall cap: patent plus SPC ≤15 years from the first EU authorisation.
+6 months for a completed paediatric investigation plan. SPCs are national.
Manufacturing waiver: make for export, or stockpile in the last 6 months, after notification.

exercises.scenario: A basic patent was filed in 2010; the first EU authorisation came in 2017.

questions.prompt: How long can the SPC be, before any paediatric extension?
options: No SPC, since less than 10 years passed
7 years, the full time to authorisation
2 years
5 years, the cap
questions.explanation: 7 − 5 = 2; the patent expires 2030, the SPC 2032, within the 15-year cap.

questions.prompt: The originator completed its paediatric plan. What changes?
options: The patent gets 2 more years
The SPC gets 6 more months
Market protection gets 1 more year
Nothing for generics
questions.explanation: The paediatric extension.

exercises.scenario: The SPC in Germany ends on 30 June 2029. You want stock on shelves on 1 July.

questions.prompt: What lets you make that stock in the EU beforehand?
options: Nothing; manufacturing must wait until the day after expiry
The Bolar exemption, which covers stockpiling at any time
A compulsory licence from the national patent office, granted on request
The SPC manufacturing waiver, from January 2029, with notifications
questions.explanation: Last 6 months only, notifying the patent office and SPC holder in advance.

questions.prompt: Portugal has no SPC for this product. What follows?
options: Portugal's date may be earlier than Germany's
Portugal can't approve the generic
Portugal follows the German SPC date
The SPC applies EU-wide anyway
questions.explanation: SPCs are granted country by country.

summary.title: Exclusivity vs patents
points: Regulatory protection (medicines law, agencies) and patents/SPCs (patent law, courts) run separately.
Earliest launch = latest of market protection end, every infringed patent's expiry, SPC (+ paediatric) expiry.
Dates can differ by country, since patents and SPCs are national.
No patent linkage in the EU: agencies don't refuse licences because of patents.
File early, but never treat the licence date as the launch date.

exercises.scenario: Market protection ends in 2027; the licence comes in 2027; the SPC expires in 2029.

questions.prompt: When can you launch, absent litigation?
options: 2031, adding the paediatric extension automatically
2028, halfway between
2027, when the licence is granted
questions.explanation: The latest date wins.

questions.prompt: Could the agency have refused the licence because of the SPC?
options: Only in a decentralised procedure
Only if the SPC holder objects within 60 days
No: there's no patent linkage in the EU
Yes: agencies always check SPCs before granting
questions.explanation: Courts enforce patents, not agencies.

exercises.scenario: Your licence was granted, and sales wants to ship next week while a patent is still in force.

questions.prompt: What's the problem?
options: A licence doesn't give the right to launch while a patent applies
Only the price must be approved first; the patent is the agency's concern
The licence is invalid while the patent runs
None; the licence overrides the patent
questions.explanation: Holding a licence isn't the same as being allowed to launch.

questions.prompt: Who enforces the patent clock?
options: The national agency
Courts
The EMA
The CMDh
questions.explanation: Agencies apply regulatory protection only.

summary.title: The Bolar exemption
points: Bolar: studies and steps needed for generic approval don't infringe patents or SPCs.
Today in Art. 10(6), written into each country's law with differences; pricing and tenders unclear in some.
Reform: explicitly covers authorisations, HTA, pricing and reimbursement, and tenders.
Never covers selling before expiry; stockpiling only via the SPC waiver's last 6 months.
Today, ask counsel country by country; after the reform these steps can run in parallel.

exercises.scenario: The SPC runs until 2028. You want to run the BE study in 2025 and submit a tender bid in 2027.

questions.prompt: Which is clearly covered today in every EU country?
options: Both, in every EU country
Submitting the tender bid for delivery after expiry
Neither, until the SPC ends
The BE study and getting the licence
questions.explanation: Tenders are unclear in some countries today.

questions.prompt: What do you do about the tender?
options: Wait until the reform is adopted
Submit it, since Bolar covers all steps
Ask patent counsel for that country
Ask the agency for permission
questions.explanation: Country-by-country practice differs today.

exercises.scenario: After the reform applies, a colleague says 'Bolar now lets us sell three months early'.

questions.prompt: Is that right?
options: No: selling before expiry is still infringement
Only in countries without an SPC
Yes: the reform allows sales in the last three months
Yes, but only through tenders won in advance
questions.explanation: Bolar covers preparation, never sale.

questions.prompt: What does the reform bring forward?
options: The SPC expiry date itself, by up to six months for every product
HTA, pricing and tender steps can run in parallel with the patent clock
The manufacturing waiver window to 12 months
The data protection period
questions.explanation: That can bring launches forward.

summary.title: Freedom to operate
points: FTO: can this product launch in these countries without infringing valid patents?
Four ways: clear, design around, challenge, licence or wait.
EPO opposition within 9 months of grant decides validity for all countries at once.
Owned by patent counsel; BD and RA supply product details.
Get it before committing launch stock; update it if formulation or process changes.

exercises.scenario: The compound SPC ends in 2028, but a formulation patent blocks your tablet until 2031.

questions.prompt: What could bring launch back to 2028?
options: Using the Bolar exemption
Designing around it, or a successful challenge
Filing the licence application earlier than planned
Choosing a different RMS
questions.explanation: Two of the four ways forward.

questions.prompt: The patent was granted five months ago. Which option is open now?
options: An EPO opposition
A preliminary injunction against the patent holder
A paediatric extension
An informed-consent application
questions.explanation: Possible within 9 months of grant, covering all countries.

exercises.scenario: The manufacturer switches the granulation process after the FTO was signed off.

questions.prompt: What must the PM do?
options: Ask RA to file a Type IA variation
Nothing; FTOs cover all future changes
Get the FTO updated before committing stock
Nothing: an FTO opinion covers later process changes automatically
questions.explanation: Process changes can bring a process patent into play.

questions.prompt: How should the FTO opinion appear on the plan?
options: As an optional deliverable after launch
Only in the risk register
As part of the national phase
As a launch gate
questions.explanation: A late FTO can move the launch.

summary.title: Launch at risk
points: Launch at risk: selling before a patent expires, believing it's invalid or not infringed.
If the patent is upheld: stop selling and pay damages.
Preliminary injunctions stop sales fast; how easily varies by country.
Since June 2023 the UPC can rule for all participating states at once.
Management decides on legal advice; the PM plans scenarios, with stock and tenders able to stop or start.

exercises.scenario: Management is considering a launch at risk in Germany and the Netherlands.

questions.prompt: What's the PM's role?
options: Lay out dates, conditions and scenarios
Decide whether to launch, based on the plan
Assess the patent's validity
Negotiate with the patent holder
questions.explanation: Management decides, on legal advice.

questions.prompt: What does the UPC change for this decision?
options: Injunctions become impossible, as the UPC decides only on validity
One ruling can stop sales in both countries at once
It removes the risk of damages entirely
It only applies to compound patents
questions.explanation: Since June 2023, for participating states.

exercises.scenario: Your plan shows a single launch date for this product.

questions.prompt: What should it show instead?
options: The date the patent was granted
A later date to be safe
The licence date, since the injunction risk can't be planned
Scenarios, for example with and without an injunction
questions.explanation: Plan scenarios, not one date.

questions.prompt: What must be able to change quickly?
options: The QPPV
The marketing authorisation
Stock, artworks and tenders
The legal basis
questions.explanation: So you can stop or start fast.

summary.title: Trademarks and invented names
points: Name: an invented name, or the common name (usually the INN) with a trademark or the MAH's name.
Two checks: trademark clearance (legal) and confusion check by the agency (safety).
EMA checks for centralised products; each agency in national procedures.
Many generics use INN + company name: faster and less risk of rejection.
In a DCP the name may differ by country, which affects artworks.

exercises.scenario: Marketing proposes the invented name 'Rosuvo' for a rosuvastatin generic.

questions.prompt: What must happen before filing?
options: A BE study under the new name
Trademark clearance
A Type II variation
Approval by the CMDh
questions.explanation: And the agency can still reject it.

questions.prompt: What does the agency check?
options: That it appears on the WHO's list of International Nonproprietary Names
That it's registered at the EUIPO
That it can't be confused with another medicine, written or spoken
That it's shorter than the INN
questions.explanation: A patient-safety check.

exercises.scenario: In your DCP, Spain rejects the invented name but France accepts it.

questions.prompt: What's the knock-on effect?
options: Different names by country, so separate artworks
France must also reject it
Nothing; the name isn't on the pack
The whole DCP must restart
questions.explanation: The name may differ from country to country.

questions.prompt: What would have avoided this?
options: A longer clock-stop
Filing the name with the EPO
Choosing Spain as RMS
Using INN + company name
questions.explanation: Faster and safer for most generics.

summary.title: Patents, SPCs and the launch date
points: Patents layer on compound, salt, formulation, process and use; only the compound can't be avoided.
SPC: filing to first authorisation minus 5, cap 5, total ≤15 years; +6 months paediatric.
Earliest launch: the latest of market protection, patent and SPC dates, country by country.
No patent linkage: a licence isn't permission to launch.
Bolar covers preparation; the SPC waiver covers stockpiling in the last 6 months.

exercises.scenario: Basic patent filed 2009, first EU authorisation 2016, paediatric plan completed. Market protection ends 2026.

questions.prompt: When does the SPC end?
options: 2026, with market protection
2034, with the full 5-year cap
Mid-2031: patent 2029, SPC 2 years, plus 6 months
End-2029, when the patent ends, since no SPC applies here
questions.explanation: 7 − 5 = 2 years, then the paediatric 6 months; within the 15-year cap.

questions.prompt: When can stockpiling for EU launch start?
options: Two years before expiry, under Bolar
Only after expiry
Any time after the licence is granted
Six months before SPC expiry, after notification
questions.explanation: The SPC manufacturing waiver.

questions.prompt: Explain why a valid licence may still not let you launch.
questions.modelAnswer: In the EU, agencies don't check patents (no patent linkage). Patents and SPCs are enforced separately by courts, so you can hold a licence and still be blocked until they expire.

exercises.scenario: Two countries in your DCP: Germany has an SPC to 2030, Poland has none.

questions.prompt: What's your launch plan?
options: Poland at market protection end if no other patent applies; Germany in 2030
Neither until the German SPC ends
Both in 2030, to keep the DCP together
Both at market protection end
questions.explanation: Patents and SPCs are national.

questions.prompt: Which preparation is clearly allowed before 2030 in Germany?
options: Advertising the generic to doctors
The studies and steps to get the licence
Selling to hospitals at a discount
Shipping stock to wholesalers in 2029
questions.explanation: Bolar covers approval steps.

summary.title: Clearing the way to launch
points: FTO per product and country: clear, design around, challenge, licence or wait.
EPO opposition within 9 months of grant covers all countries.
Launch at risk: management's call; injunctions and the UPC can stop several markets.
Names: INN + company name avoids trademark and confusion problems.
Master grid: one row per country; the latest date is the earliest launch.

exercises.scenario: FTO flags a crystal-form patent to 2030; the SPC ends 2028. Management asks for options.

questions.prompt: Which options do you put on the slide?
options: File a variation to extend the SPC
Ask the agency to set the patent aside
Launch in 2028 since only the SPC counts
Design around the form, challenge it, licence, or wait to 2030
questions.explanation: The four ways forward.

questions.prompt: If they choose a launch at risk, what do you plan?
options: Scenarios with and without an injunction
Only the 2030 date
A new legal basis
One date, 2028, and no change to stock, artwork or tender plans
questions.explanation: Stock and tenders must be able to stop or start.

questions.prompt: Who owns each date in the master grid?
questions.modelAnswer: RA owns market protection dates; patent counsel owns patent, SPC and FTO dates; BD supplies the target countries and product details.

exercises.scenario: A new formulation is introduced to design around the patent.

questions.prompt: What has to be refreshed?
options: Only the trademark
Nothing; design-arounds are automatic
The FTO and the regulatory dossier
Only the artwork
questions.explanation: Design-arounds usually need regulatory work, and the FTO must cover the new product.

questions.prompt: A patent was granted last month. What's the fastest way to test its validity across Europe?
options: A preliminary injunction
An EPO opposition
A UPC infringement action against yourself
National invalidity actions in every country
questions.explanation: One decision for all countries, within 9 months of grant.

summary.title: Intellectual property: the whole picture
points: Patents and SPCs (courts) run alongside regulatory protection (agencies); there's no linkage.
Earliest launch per country = the latest of market protection, patent and SPC (+6 months) dates.
SPC: up to 5 years, total ≤15 from first authorisation; waiver for stockpiling in the last 6 months.
Bolar covers approval steps; the reform adds HTA, pricing and tenders.
FTO is a launch gate; options are clear, design around, challenge, licence or wait.
Launch at risk is management's call; INN + company name keeps naming simple.

exercises.scenario: Market protection ends March 2028. Germany has an SPC to December 2029; country X has none. FTO is clear in both.

questions.prompt: Earliest launches?
options: Both December 2029
Both March 2028
Germany March 2028; country X December 2029
Germany December 2029; country X March 2028
questions.explanation: The latest date in each row.

questions.prompt: When can you make German day-one stock in the EU?
options: From June 2029, with notification under the SPC waiver
Only after December 2029
From March 2028, under Bolar
Any time, since the FTO is clear
questions.explanation: The last 6 months of the SPC.

questions.prompt: Which tender steps in Germany before December 2029 need counsel's advice today?
options: Filing the licence application
Answering Day 105 questions
Submitting bids for supply after expiry
Running the bioequivalence study on reference batches bought in Germany
questions.explanation: Tenders are unclear today; the reform makes them explicit.

exercises.scenario: A partner from outside the EU says 'in our country the agency won't approve a generic while the patent is in force'.

questions.prompt: How is the EU different?
options: EU agencies only check SPCs
No patent linkage: approval can come before expiry
The EU works the same way
Approval in the EU needs the patent holder's consent
questions.explanation: Courts enforce patents separately.

questions.prompt: So what's the main planning implication?
options: Wait for patent expiry before filing
Use the licence date as the launch date
File early so the licence is ready when the last clock runs out
Avoid any steps before expiry
questions.explanation: But never treat the grant date as the launch date.

questions.prompt: In two sentences, explain to management what a launch at risk exposes the company to.
questions.modelAnswer: If a court later upholds the patent, the company may have to stop selling, possibly across several countries with one UPC ruling or a preliminary injunction, and pay damages. It's management's decision on legal advice, so the PM plans scenarios that let stock and tenders stop or start fast.
